newsitem.title: CYPRUS: FEATURE - Cypriots protest plans to scrap gay ban.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Cypriots protest plans to scrap gay ban.

text.p: A move to scrap a 19th-century law banning homosexuality is upsetting the all-powerful church in Cyprus, with bearded priests and monks taking to the streets in protest.
The Cyprus government has come under pressure from the Council of Europe to decriminalise homosexuality after the European Court of Justice in 1993 sided with a Cypriot's fight to overturn the law.

But an attempt to push an amendment through parliament, or risk being ejected from the Council of Europe, has run into strong opposition from the dominant Greek Orthodox church, which says homosexuality taints traditional values.

Last week priests and monks picketed parliament holding Sodom and Gomorrah banners to remind legislators of the biblical cities that were destroyed by the wrath of God because of the perversion of their inhabitants.
A larger number plan a mass protest again when parliament meets to take a firm position on the bill.
CHURCH SET AGAINST BILL

"Decriminalisation of homosexuality will deal a blow to marriage and family...it will encourage perversion and debauchery and will have as a result the further spread of various infectuous diseases like AIDS," railed the Holy Synod, the governing body of the Church of Cyprus, in a circular read out in churches on Sunday.
Scrapping the controversial law, promulgated in 1889, will allow sex between consenting male adults. The old law made no reference to females.
Only one political party has openly come out against the bill -- the centre-right Democratic Party, which has 10 of 56 seats in the House of Representatives.

"Our party will reject the decriminalisation of homosexuality and we are ready to face the consequences of this stand," said Nicos Pittocopitis, a deputy for the Democratic Party and a voiciferous anti-homosexual campaigner.
He insisted that restoring the human rights of Cypriots affected by the Turkish invasion was a priority for his party and not the "alleged" violation of rights of homosexuals.
Turkey has occupied northern Cyprus since 1974 after a brief Greek Cypriot coup in capital Nicosia sparked by the military then ruling Greece. Close to 200,000 people were displaced.
"Homosexuals are not prosecuted. Not one case has gone to court," Pittocopitis told Reuters.
GAYS CITE VIOLATION OF RIGHTS
But Alecos Modinos, the Nicosia architect and gay rights activist who went to the European Court four years ago claiming the 1889 law violated his human rights, says its mere existence is bad enough.
"In the eyes of the law I'm a criminal and society stigmatises me," he said.
The small United Democrats party, with two deputies, supports the bill. But the remaining three parties have avoided taking a clear stand, indicating it may boil down to voting by conscience.
Sociologist Nicos Peristianis said there may be voices in the Greek Cypriot population of 625,000 afraid to openly back the bill.
"I think males are afraid to talk because they think their own masculinity will be questioned if they come out in support of decriminalisation," he added.
"Cypriots are conservative and on this subject there is no great sensitivity so they don't risk a lot by not taking a stand."
Modinos, head of the Cyprus gay liberation movement, said that in addition to the perceived discrimination shown by the church, there was discrimination in the workplace.
"A lot of businesses wouldn't employ us if they knew of our sexual orientation," he explained.
Modinos said he did not know how many gays there were in the Greek Cypriot community, but it was generally accepted that in most societies 10 percent of the population was homosexual.
